topic.subject: science
topic.title: Air around us
topic.scope: composition of air, oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, water vapour, air takes up space, air for living things

nodes.name: Empty containers are full of air

misconceptions.statement: An empty glass contains nothing at all.
misconceptions.why: Air is invisible and cannot be felt when it is still.
misconceptions.fix: Even an 'empty' glass is filled with air, which can be proven by trying to push an inverted glass into water.

probe.question: If you push an empty glass upside down into a bucket of water, why doesn't water enter it immediately?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the glass is empty and water is heavy.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: Air has no weight because it floats.
misconceptions.why: Students associate weight only with heavy, solid objects that they can feel.
misconceptions.fix: Air is matter and has mass; a balloon filled with air weighs more than a deflated one.

probe.question: Which is heavier: a flat football or the same football pumped up with air?
probe.wrong_answer: They both weigh the same because air has no weight.

misconceptions.root_belief: gases have no mass or weight
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

misconceptions.statement: Soil is a solid block with no space for air.
misconceptions.why: Soil looks like a continuous solid mass to the naked eye.
misconceptions.fix: Soil contains tiny spaces between its particles that are filled with air, which escapes as bubbles when water is added.

probe.question: Why do bubbles come out when you pour water on a lump of dry soil?
probe.wrong_answer: The water is boiling or reacting with the soil.

misconceptions.root_belief: solids are continuous and have no internal space

misconceptions.statement: Fish breathe the oxygen atoms that are part of the water molecules (H2O).
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the chemical composition of water with dissolved gases.
misconceptions.fix: Fish breathe oxygen gas that is dissolved in water, not the oxygen that is chemically bonded to hydrogen in water molecules.

probe.question: Where do fish get the oxygen they need to breathe?
probe.wrong_answer: They break apart water molecules to get oxygen.

misconceptions.root_belief: chemical components are the same as mixtures

misconceptions.statement: Air is mostly made of oxygen because we need it to survive.
misconceptions.why: Students assume the most important gas for life must be the most abundant.
misconceptions.fix: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the air, while oxygen is only about 21%.

probe.question: Which gas is the most abundant in the air around us?

misconceptions.statement: Oxygen itself catches fire and burns.
misconceptions.fix: Oxygen helps other things burn but does not burn itself.

probe.question: If you light a match in a room full of pure oxygen, what happens?
probe.wrong_answer: The oxygen gas catches fire and explodes.

misconceptions.root_belief: a facilitator of a process is the same as the fuel

misconceptions.statement: Carbon dioxide is only a waste product and has no use in nature.
misconceptions.why: Textbooks often focus on CO2 as a pollutant or a waste product of respiration.
misconceptions.fix: Carbon dioxide is essential for plants to make food through photosynthesis.

probe.question: Is carbon dioxide useful for anything in the atmosphere?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is just a harmful gas that causes pollution.

misconceptions.statement: Water vapour only exists in the air when it is raining or humid.
misconceptions.why: Water vapour is invisible, so students only acknowledge it when it condenses into visible droplets.
misconceptions.fix: Water vapour is always present in the air, though the amount varies by location and weather.

probe.question: Where does the water on the outside of a cold glass come from on a dry day?
probe.wrong_answer: It leaks through the glass from the inside.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: Plants breathe in carbon dioxide and breathe out oxygen, but they do not respire like animals.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the gas exchange of photosynthesis with the process of respiration.
misconceptions.fix: Plants respire all the time (taking in oxygen and releasing CO2), just like animals; photosynthesis only happens in light.

probe.question: What gas do plants take in during the night when there is no sunlight?

misconceptions.root_belief: one organism performs only one gas exchange process

misconceptions.statement: Plants produce oxygen specifically so that animals can breathe.
misconceptions.why: A teleological view of nature where everything exists for a human or animal purpose.
misconceptions.fix: Oxygen is a byproduct of the plant's food-making process; plants do not 'intend' to provide for animals.

probe.question: Why do plants release oxygen into the air?
probe.wrong_answer: To make sure animals don't die.

misconceptions.root_belief: natural processes have a human-centric purpose
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

misconceptions.statement: Air only exists when the wind is blowing.
misconceptions.why: We only feel the physical force of air when it is in motion.
misconceptions.fix: Air is a substance that is present even when it is perfectly still and we cannot feel it.

probe.question: Is there air in a closed room where no fan is running and no wind is blowing?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the air is gone because there is no wind.

misconceptions.root_belief: movement is a requirement for existence

misconceptions.statement: Smoke is a gas, just like oxygen or nitrogen.
misconceptions.why: Smoke floats and spreads like a gas, and its individual particles are too small to see clearly.
misconceptions.fix: Smoke is a mixture of gases and tiny solid particles (soot/ash).

probe.question: If you filter smoke through a fine cloth, why does it leave a black stain?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the gas turned into a solid on the cloth.

misconceptions.root_belief: if it floats and spreads it must be a gas

misconceptions.statement: The atmosphere is a very thick layer that goes on forever into space.
misconceptions.why: The sky looks infinitely high to a child looking up.
misconceptions.fix: The atmosphere is a relatively thin layer of air surrounding the Earth, becoming thinner as we go higher.

probe.question: Does the amount of air stay the same as you climb a very high mountain?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, air is everywhere in space.

misconceptions.statement: Nitrogen is 'useless' air because we don't use it for breathing.
misconceptions.why: Students often categorize things as 'useful' or 'useless' based solely on human respiration.
misconceptions.fix: Nitrogen is vital for plant growth and it also prevents fires from burning out of control by diluting oxygen.

probe.question: What would happen if the air was 100% oxygen instead of having nitrogen?
probe.wrong_answer: It would be better because we could breathe more easily.

misconceptions.root_belief: a thing has only one function
